# Introduction to the particulate nature of matter
## Elements, compounds and mixtures
An element is a substance made of only one type of atom. A compound is two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio. A mixture is two or more substances physically combined; it can be homogeneous, with uniform composition, or heterogeneous. Mixtures are separated by physical methods such as filtration, crystallization, distillation, paper chromatography and evaporation.

## States of matter
The kinetic molecular theory describes matter as particles in constant motion. Solids have particles vibrating in fixed positions; liquids have particles close together but able to move; gases have particles far apart moving randomly. Changes of state include melting, freezing, boiling, condensation, sublimation and deposition. Temperature in kelvin is proportional to the average kinetic energy of the particles.

## Key terms
Element: a substance made of only one type of atom
Compound: elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio
Mixture: substances physically combined
Homogeneous mixture: a mixture with uniform composition
Sublimation: a change directly from solid to gas
Kinetic molecular theory: the model of matter as moving particles
The nuclear atom:
# The nuclear atom
## Atomic structure
Atoms contain a nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons. Protons have a relative charge of +1 and mass 1; neutrons have charge 0 and mass 1; electrons have charge −1 and negligible mass. The atomic number Z is the number of protons. The mass number A is the number of protons plus neutrons.

## Isotopes and mass spectrometry
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. They have the same chemical properties but different physical properties. Relative atomic mass is the weighted average mass of an element's isotopes compared with one-twelfth of carbon-12. A mass spectrometer measures the masses and abundances of isotopes.

## Key terms
Atomic number: the number of protons in the nucleus
Mass number: the number of protons plus neutrons
Isotope: atoms of an element with different numbers of neutrons
Relative atomic mass: the weighted average mass of an element’s isotopes
Mass spectrometer: an instrument that measures isotope masses and abundances
Electron configurations:
# Electron configurations
## Energy levels
Electrons occupy energy levels (shells), sub-levels (s, p, d, f) and orbitals. An orbital is a region of space that holds up to two electrons with opposite spins. The aufbau principle states that electrons fill the lowest energy orbitals first. Hund's rule states that electrons occupy orbitals of the same sub-level singly before pairing. The Pauli exclusion principle states that no two electrons in an atom have the same set of quantum numbers.

## Spectra and ionization
An emission spectrum is produced when excited electrons fall to lower energy levels and emit photons. The hydrogen line spectrum converges at higher frequencies. First ionization energy is the energy needed to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms. Successive ionization energies give evidence for shells and sub-levels.

## Key terms
Orbital: a region holding up to two electrons
Aufbau principle: electrons fill the lowest energy orbitals first
Hund’s rule: electrons fill orbitals singly before pairing
Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons have the same set of quantum numbers
First ionization energy: the energy to remove a mole of electrons from gaseous atoms
Emission spectrum: lines of light emitted as electrons fall to lower levels
Counting particles by mass: the mole:
# Counting particles by mass: the mole
## The mole
The mole is the amount of substance that contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles, the Avogadro constant. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance, in g mol⁻¹. The amount in moles is n = m/M.

## Formulas and concentration
The empirical formula is the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. The molecular formula gives the actual number of atoms of each element in a molecule. Concentration is the amount of solute per volume of solution, c = n/V, in mol dm⁻³. A standard solution has a known concentration. Titration is a technique to find an unknown concentration using a standard solution.

## Key terms
Mole: the amount containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles
Avogadro constant: 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹
Molar mass: the mass of one mole of a substance
Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms
Molecular formula: the actual number of atoms of each element
Concentration: amount of solute per volume of solution
Ideal gases:
# Ideal gases
## Ideal gas behaviour
An ideal gas is a model in which particles have no volume and no intermolecular forces, and collisions are perfectly elastic. Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature, when particle volume and attractions matter.

## Gas laws
The ideal gas equation is pV = nRT, with p in Pa, V in m³, T in K and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of particles. Molar volume at STP (273 K, 100 kPa) is 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹. The combined gas law is p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂.

## Key terms
Ideal gas: a model gas with no particle volume or attractions
Ideal gas equation: pV = nRT
Molar volume: the volume of one mole of gas, 22.7 dm³ at STP
Avogadro’s law: equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles
STP: standard temperature and pressure, 273 K and 100 kPa
The ionic model:
# The ionic model
## Ionic bonding
An ion is an atom or group of atoms with an electric charge. Cations are positive ions formed when metals lose electrons; anions are negative ions formed when non-metals gain electrons. An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Ionic compounds form a lattice, a regular three-dimensional arrangement of ions.

## Properties
Ionic compounds have high melting points because strong forces hold the lattice together. They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved, because the ions are free to move, but not when solid. They are often soluble in water and brittle. Lattice enthalpy is a measure of the strength of an ionic lattice; it increases with ion charge and decreases with ion size.

## Key terms
Ion: a charged atom or group of atoms
Cation: a positive ion
Anion: a negative ion
Ionic bond: electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
Lattice: a regular 3D arrangement of particles
Lattice enthalpy: a measure of the strength of an ionic lattice
The covalent model:
# The covalent model
## Covalent bonding
A covalent bond is the electrostatic attraction between a shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the bonded atoms. Single, double and triple bonds share one, two and three pairs. A coordination bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons come from one atom. Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons; unequal sharing makes a polar bond.

## Shapes and forces
VSEPR theory states that electron domains around a central atom repel to be as far apart as possible, giving shapes such as linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, bent and trigonal pyramidal. Intermolecular forces include London dispersion forces, dipole–dipole forces and hydrogen bonds. Covalent network structures, such as diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide, have very high melting points. Resonance structures describe delocalized electrons.

## Key terms
Covalent bond: attraction between a shared electron pair and two nuclei
Electronegativity: an atom’s ability to attract a shared electron pair
VSEPR theory: electron domains repel to be as far apart as possible
Hydrogen bond: a strong intermolecular force between H and N, O or F
London dispersion forces: weak forces from temporary dipoles
Coordination bond: a covalent bond where both electrons come from one atom
The metallic model:
# The metallic model
## Metallic bonding
A metallic bond is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of cations and a sea of delocalized electrons. The strength of metallic bonding increases with the charge of the cations and decreases with their size.

## Properties and alloys
Metals conduct electricity and heat because delocalized electrons move freely. They are malleable and ductile because layers of cations can slide without breaking the bonding. An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements; different-sized atoms disrupt the layers, making alloys harder and stronger than the pure metal. Transition elements have variable oxidation states and form coloured compounds.

## Key terms
Metallic bond: attraction between cations and delocalized electrons
Delocalized electrons: electrons free to move through a structure
Malleable: able to be hammered into shape
Ductile: able to be drawn into wires
Alloy: a mixture of a metal with other elements
From models to materials:
# From models to materials
## The bonding triangle
The bonding triangle (van Arkel–Ketelaar diagram) classifies bonding as ionic, covalent or metallic using the average electronegativity and the difference in electronegativity of the elements. Most bonding lies on a continuum between the three types.

## Materials
Polymers are large molecules made of repeating units called monomers. Addition polymers form from alkenes when the double bond breaks. Condensation polymers form with the loss of a small molecule, such as water, as in polyesters and polyamides. The properties of materials, such as strength, conductivity and melting point, can be explained from their bonding and structure.

## Key terms
Bonding triangle: a diagram classifying bonding by electronegativity
Polymer: a large molecule of repeating units
Monomer: a small molecule that joins to form a polymer
Addition polymer: a polymer formed from alkenes without losing atoms
Condensation polymer: a polymer formed with loss of a small molecule
The periodic table: classification of el:
# The periodic table: classification of elements
## Organization
The periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number. A period is a horizontal row; a group is a vertical column. Elements are in s, p, d and f blocks according to their outer sub-level. Metals are on the left, non-metals on the right, and metalloids between.

## Periodic trends
Atomic radius decreases across a period because nuclear charge increases, and increases down a group because of more shells. Ionization energy and electronegativity increase across a period and decrease down a group. Group 1 metals become more reactive down the group; group 17 halogens become less reactive down the group. Oxides of metals are basic and oxides of non-metals are acidic. An oxidation state is the charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic.

## Key terms
Period: a horizontal row of the periodic table
Group: a vertical column of the periodic table
Atomic radius: the size of an atom
Halogen: an element in group 17
Oxidation state: the charge an atom would have if all bonds were ionic
Metalloid: an element with properties between metals and non-metals
Functional groups: classification of org:
# Functional groups: classification of organic compounds
## Organic compounds
A homologous series is a family of compounds with the same functional group and general formula, differing by CH₂. A functional group is the atom or group of atoms that gives a compound its characteristic reactions. Examples include alkanes, alkenes, alcohols (–OH), aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids (–COOH), esters, amines and halogenoalkanes.

## Naming and isomers
IUPAC nomenclature names compounds by the longest carbon chain and its functional groups. Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols have the –OH carbon bonded to one, two or three other carbons. Stereoisomers have the same structure but a different arrangement in space, such as cis–trans and optical isomers.

## Key terms
Homologous series: a family of compounds with the same functional group
Functional group: the part of a molecule that gives its characteristic reactions
Structural isomer: same molecular formula, different structure
IUPAC nomenclature: the systematic naming of compounds
Stereoisomer: same structure but a different arrangement in space
Measuring enthalpy changes:
# Measuring enthalpy changes
## Enthalpy
Enthalpy change ΔH is the heat energy exchanged with the surroundings at constant pressure. An exothermic reaction releases heat, so ΔH is negative and the surroundings warm up. An endothermic reaction absorbs heat, so ΔH is positive.

## Calorimetry
Calorimetry measures enthalpy changes using q = mcΔT, where m is the mass of the water or solution, c its specific heat capacity and ΔT the temperature change. Then ΔH = −q/n. Errors include heat loss to the surroundings and incomplete combustion. Standard enthalpy changes are measured at 100 kPa and 298 K.

## Key terms
Enthalpy change: heat exchanged at constant pressure, ΔH
Exothermic reaction: a reaction that releases heat, ΔH negative
Endothermic reaction: a reaction that absorbs heat, ΔH positive
Calorimetry: measuring enthalpy changes from temperature changes
Specific heat capacity: energy to raise 1 g by 1 K
Energy cycles in reactions:
# Energy cycles in reactions
## Bond enthalpies
Bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of a bond in gaseous molecules. Bond breaking is endothermic and bond making is exothermic. ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). Average bond enthalpies give approximate values.

## Hess's law
Hess's law states that the total enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken. Energy cycles use enthalpies of formation or combustion to calculate unknown values. The standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states. A Born–Haber cycle is an energy cycle for forming an ionic compound.

## Key terms
Bond enthalpy: energy to break one mole of a bond in gaseous molecules
Hess’s law: the enthalpy change is independent of the route
Enthalpy of formation: enthalpy change forming one mole from elements
Born–Haber cycle: an energy cycle for forming an ionic compound
Enthalpy of combustion: enthalpy change burning one mole completely in oxygen
Energy from fuels:
# Energy from fuels
## Combustion
Combustion is a reaction of a fuel with oxygen that releases energy. Complete combustion of hydrocarbons produces carbon dioxide and water; incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide or carbon (soot) as well. Fossil fuels such as coal, oil and natural gas are non-renewable.

## Alternatives
Biofuels are fuels produced from living matter, such as ethanol from fermentation. Specific energy is the energy released per unit mass of a fuel; energy density is the energy released per unit volume. A fuel cell converts chemical energy directly into electrical energy using a redox reaction. Burning fuels releases greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.

## Key terms
Combustion: reaction of a fuel with oxygen releasing energy
Incomplete combustion: burning with too little oxygen, giving CO or soot
Biofuel: a fuel produced from living matter
Specific energy: energy released per unit mass of fuel
Fuel cell: a device converting chemical energy directly to electricity
Entropy and spontaneity:
# Entropy and spontaneity
## Entropy
Entropy S is a measure of the dispersal of energy and matter, or disorder, in a system. Gases have higher entropy than liquids, which have higher entropy than solids. ΔS is positive when the number of gas particles increases.

## Gibbs energy
Gibbs energy change ΔG = ΔH − TΔS determines whether a reaction is spontaneous. A reaction is spontaneous if ΔG is negative. A reaction with negative ΔH and positive ΔS is spontaneous at all temperatures. ΔG is related to the equilibrium constant by ΔG° = −RT ln K.

## Key terms
Entropy: a measure of energy and matter dispersal
Gibbs energy change: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
Spontaneous reaction: a reaction with negative ΔG
ΔG° and K: ΔG° = −RT ln K
How much? The amount of chemical change:
# How much? The amount of chemical change
## Equations and stoichiometry
A balanced chemical equation shows the same number of each type of atom on both sides. Stoichiometry is the use of mole ratios from balanced equations to calculate amounts. The limiting reactant is the reactant that is used up first and limits the amount of product; the other is in excess.

## Yield and economy
Theoretical yield is the maximum product possible. Percentage yield is the actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, times 100%. Atom economy is the mass of the desired product divided by the total mass of all products, times 100%; high atom economy means less waste.

## Key terms
Stoichiometry: using mole ratios to calculate amounts
Limiting reactant: the reactant used up first
Theoretical yield: the maximum amount of product possible
Percentage yield: actual yield divided by theoretical yield, times 100%
Atom economy: mass of desired product over mass of all products, times 100%
How fast? The rate of chemical change:
# How fast? The rate of chemical change
## Rate of reaction
Rate of reaction is the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. Collision theory states that particles must collide with enough energy and the correct orientation to react. Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for a reaction.

## Factors
Rate increases with temperature, concentration, pressure and surface area, and with a catalyst. A catalyst increases the rate by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and is not used up. The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution shows the energies of particles. At HL, the rate equation rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ gives the order of reaction, and the Arrhenius equation k = Ae^(−Ea/RT) links rate constant and temperature.

## Key terms
Rate of reaction: change in concentration per unit time
Collision theory: particles must collide with enough energy and correct orientation
Activation energy: the minimum energy needed to react
Catalyst: a substance that speeds up a reaction by lowering activation energy
Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution: a graph of particle energies
Rate equation: rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ
How far? The extent of chemical change:
# How far? The extent of chemical change
## Dynamic equilibrium
Dynamic equilibrium is the state of a reversible reaction in a closed system where the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stay constant. The equilibrium constant Kc is the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations, each raised to the power of its coefficient. A large K means the equilibrium lies to the right.

## Le Chatelier's principle
Le Chatelier's principle states that if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the position of equilibrium shifts to oppose the change. Increasing concentration of a reactant shifts it to the right; increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles; increasing temperature favours the endothermic direction. Only temperature changes K. A catalyst does not change the position of equilibrium. The reaction quotient Q compared with K predicts the direction of change.

## Key terms
Dynamic equilibrium: forward and reverse rates equal in a closed system
Equilibrium constant: Kc, the ratio of products to reactants at equilibrium
Le Chatelier’s principle: an equilibrium shifts to oppose a change
Reaction quotient: Q, the ratio calculated at any moment
Closed system: a system where no matter enters or leaves
Proton transfer reactions:
# Proton transfer reactions
## Acids and bases
A Brønsted–Lowry acid is a proton donor; a Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton acceptor. A conjugate acid–base pair differs by one proton. Strong acids dissociate completely in water; weak acids dissociate partially. Amphiprotic species can both donate and accept protons, like water.

## pH
pH is −log[H⁺]. A pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is alkaline at 25 °C. The ionic product of water is Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. Neutralization is the reaction of an acid with a base to form a salt and water. A buffer solution resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added. An indicator changes colour at the equivalence point of a titration.

## Key terms
Brønsted–Lowry acid: a proton donor
Brønsted–Lowry base: a proton acceptor
Conjugate acid–base pair: two species differing by one proton
Strong acid: an acid that dissociates completely
pH: −log[H⁺]
Buffer solution: a solution that resists changes in pH
Electron transfer reactions:
# Electron transfer reactions
## Redox
Oxidation is the loss of electrons or an increase in oxidation state; reduction is the gain of electrons or a decrease in oxidation state (OIL RIG). A redox reaction involves both. An oxidizing agent accepts electrons and is reduced; a reducing agent donates electrons and is oxidized.

## Cells
A voltaic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy from a spontaneous redox reaction; oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode. An electrolytic cell uses electrical energy to drive a non-spontaneous reaction. The standard electrode potential E° measures the tendency of a half-cell to be reduced, against the standard hydrogen electrode. Cell potential is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode.

## Key terms
Oxidation: loss of electrons
Reduction: gain of electrons
Oxidizing agent: a species that accepts electrons and is reduced
Voltaic cell: a cell producing electricity from a spontaneous redox reaction
Electrolytic cell: a cell using electricity to drive a reaction
Anode: the electrode where oxidation happens
Electron sharing reactions:
# Electron sharing reactions
## Radicals
A radical is a species with an unpaired electron. Radicals form by homolytic fission, in which a covalent bond breaks and each atom takes one electron. Radicals are very reactive.

## Radical substitution
Alkanes react with halogens in ultraviolet light by radical substitution. The mechanism has three stages: initiation, where UV light splits the halogen into radicals; propagation, where radicals react with molecules and produce new radicals; and termination, where two radicals combine. The product is a mixture of halogenoalkanes. Ozone depletion by CFCs also involves radicals.

## Key terms
Radical: a species with an unpaired electron
Homolytic fission: bond breaking where each atom takes one electron
Initiation: the step that forms radicals
Propagation: steps where radicals produce new radicals
Termination: the step where two radicals combine
Electron-pair sharing reactions:
# Electron-pair sharing reactions
## Nucleophiles and electrophiles
A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor, such as OH⁻ or NH₃. An electrophile is an electron-pair acceptor, such as H⁺ or NO₂⁺. Heterolytic fission is bond breaking in which one atom takes both electrons, forming ions. Curly arrows show the movement of electron pairs in mechanisms.

## Mechanisms
Nucleophilic substitution replaces a halogen in a halogenoalkane with a nucleophile; SN1 goes through a carbocation and is typical of tertiary halogenoalkanes, SN2 happens in one step and is typical of primary ones. Electrophilic addition adds across the double bond of an alkene, such as bromine or HBr. A Lewis acid is an electron-pair acceptor and a Lewis base an electron-pair donor.

## Key terms
Nucleophile: an electron-pair donor
Electrophile: an electron-pair acceptor
Heterolytic fission: bond breaking where one atom takes both electrons
Nucleophilic substitution: replacing a group with a nucleophile
Electrophilic addition: adding across a double bond via an electrophile
Lewis acid: an electron-pair acceptor
